questions.q: When you label your step cards by type, which type of step is the best fit for an AI step?
options: Rule steps, such as if/then decisions on plan or country
Calculate steps, such as totals, dates and percentages
Read steps, such as extracting details from messy text
Judge steps, such as approving refunds or setting prices
questions.explain: Read steps, like extracting details and classifying, are best handled by an AI step. Rules go to filters or routers, calculations to formulas, and judge steps stay with a human.

questions.q: While mapping an invoice chase, a colleague calls the choice between a friendly and a firm reminder a judgment call. Pressed, they say it depends on days overdue and reminders already sent. What should you do?
options: Write it down as a rule and handle it with a router, not AI
Keep it as a judge step and have a human choose every time
Hand the decision to an AI step, since it involves tone
Drop the choice and send the same reminder to everyone
questions.explain: Many judgment steps are really rules nobody has written down. A router on days overdue and reminders sent beats AI on cost, speed and reliability.

questions.q: Your enquiry form sometimes receives submissions in another language, and you aren't sure your automation can handle them yet. Which is an acceptable way to deal with this exception?
options: Leave it off the map, since it doesn't happen very often
Wait until it breaks in production, then add a rule for it
Assume the AI step will work it out without instructions
Decide to route these submissions to a human for now
questions.explain: For every exception you decide to handle it, route it to a human, or ignore it deliberately and log it. Routing to a human is a perfectly good answer; pretending the exception doesn't exist is not.
